prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The investigation of the E. coli outbreak linked to Nestle Toll House cookie dough is nearly over, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. The cause of the contamination has not been identified. Nestle recalled all its Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products made at a Danville, Virginia, plant. David Acheson, the FDA's associate commissioner for foods, says the samples of cookie dough his agency has tested do not contain the E. coli strain that sickened 74 people in 32 states. On June 19, Nestle recalled all its Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products made at a Danville, Virginia, plant. Thirty-four people have been hospitalized; no deaths have been reported. The CDC reports that the majority of the patients were teenage girls who reported eating the cookie dough raw. Last month, the FDA found E. coli in a production sample of Toll House cookie dough, but after testing, investigators found that the strain in the sample did not match the outbreak strain. "We are still in speculation mode," Acheson said, but the E. coli "most likely came from raw ingredients" such as flour. The E.coli strain that caused the outbreak, 0157:H7, is typically found in fecal contamination from animals such as cows, sheep or goats. Acheson points out that it's not unusual for those animals to be carrying more than one strain of the bacteria. But he believes that the root cause of the contamination may never be known. "We have to conclude we're unlikely to have a definitive determination," he said. Most people with E. coli 0157:H7 experience diarrhea and abdominal cramps within eight days of infection. The FDA notified Nestle USA on Thursday that its investigation at the Danville plant was over. Nestle says FDA inspectors were at the plant for more than a week and found no E. coli on equipment. More than 1,000 tests have been conducted at the facility after the outbreak. "We've dismantled the production line and done extensive testing on all equipment and not found any E. coli," Nestle USA spokeswoman Laurie MacDonald said. MacDonald announced that Nestle is easing back into production at the plant. The company has purchased new lots of eggs, flour and margarine and says it is thoroughly testing the new products and all raw ingredients. Consumers will have to wait to see cookie dough back in grocery stores. "You're not going to see anything on the shelves for quite some time," MacDonald said. But when it does appear, the company will mark the cookie dough with a new label that clearly designates it as a new batch. It will also continue to carry a reminder to not eat the dough raw.

(CNN) — The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says its investigation into the E. coli outbreak linked to Nestlé Toll House cookie dough is nearing completion, although the source of the contamination has not been identified.

Nestlé recalled all Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products manufactured at its Danville, Virginia, plant on June 19. David Acheson, the FDA’s associate commissioner for foods, said samples of cookie dough tested by the agency did not contain the E. coli strain that sickened 74 people in 32 states. Thirty-four people have been hospitalized, and no deaths have been reported. According to the CDC, most of the patients were teenage girls who reported eating the cookie dough raw.

Last month, the FDA found E. coli in a production sample of Toll House cookie dough. However, subsequent testing showed that the strain in the sample did not match the outbreak strain.

“We are still in speculation mode,” Acheson said, adding that the E. coli “most likely came from raw ingredients,” such as flour.

The E. coli strain responsible for the outbreak, O157:H7, is typically associated with fecal contamination from animals such as cows, sheep, or goats. Acheson noted that it is not unusual for those animals to carry more than one strain of the bacteria. Still, he said the root cause of the contamination may never be known.

“We have to conclude we’re unlikely to have a definitive determination,” he said.

Most people infected with E. coli O157:H7 experience diarrhea and abdominal cramps within eight days of infection.

The FDA notified Nestlé USA on Thursday that its investigation at the Danville plant had concluded. Nestlé said FDA inspectors spent more than a week at the facility and found no E. coli on equipment. More than 1,000 tests have been conducted at the plant since the outbreak.

“We’ve dismantled the production line and done extensive testing on all equipment and not found any E. coli,” said Nestlé USA spokeswoman Laurie MacDonald.

MacDonald said Nestlé is gradually resuming production at the plant. The company has purchased new lots of eggs, flour, and margarine, and says it is thoroughly testing the new products as well as all raw ingredients.

Consumers, however, will have to wait before cookie dough returns to grocery-store shelves.

“You’re not going to see anything on the shelves for quite some time,” MacDonald said.

When the products do return, the company will mark the cookie dough with a new label clearly identifying it as a new batch. The packaging will also continue to include a reminder not to eat the dough raw.

Health officials have said the outbreak resulted in **more than 60 illnesses across multiple states**, with **about two dozen to more than 30 people hospitalized**, though no deaths were reported.

Nestlé voluntarily recalled its **Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products** in June after the FDA and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warned consumers not to eat the dough, raw or baked, because of the possible contamination risk. The recall included a wide range of refrigerated Toll House cookie dough varieties, including bars, tubs and chubs sold in grocery stores.

Investigators have focused on whether one or more **raw ingredients** may have introduced the contamination. While eggs are a common concern in raw cookie dough because of salmonella, officials have also examined ingredients such as **flour**, which is not typically treated to kill bacteria before use. FDA officials have said the manufacturing plant itself was inspected and that investigators were reviewing ingredient suppliers, production records and environmental samples.

Nestlé has said it is cooperating with federal and state investigators and emphasized that consumers should not eat raw cookie dough, even products intended to be baked before consumption. The company has also said it plans to resume production only after implementing additional safeguards.

As part of its restart plan, Nestlé said it would begin using **heat-treated flour** in refrigerated cookie dough and add further testing of ingredients and finished products. Production was expected to restart gradually once the company and regulators were satisfied that enhanced safety measures were in place.

Public health officials continue to advise consumers to discard any recalled Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough and to avoid eating any raw dough or batter, regardless of brand, because raw ingredients can carry bacteria that are killed only through proper baking.

# FDA cites concerns at Nestlé Virginia plant after Toll House cookie dough recall

**DANVILLE, Virginia** — Federal inspectors found a series of sanitation and food-safety concerns at Nestlé’s refrigerated cookie dough plant in Danville, Virginia, following a nationwide recall of Toll House cookie dough linked to an outbreak of *E. coli* illness, according to findings released by the Food and Drug Administration.

The inspection came after Nestlé voluntarily recalled its Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products amid reports that consumers had become sick after eating raw dough. Health officials warned consumers not to eat the recalled products and emphasized that cookie dough should not be consumed unless fully baked.

David Acheson, then an FDA official overseeing food safety, said the agency’s investigation focused on how contamination could have entered the product and whether conditions at the plant were adequate to prevent it. Acheson said the findings underscored the importance of strict controls in facilities producing ready-to-bake foods, particularly when consumers may eat products before cooking despite label warnings.

FDA inspectors reported issues involving plant sanitation, maintenance and procedures intended to prevent contamination. The agency’s observations did not necessarily identify a single source of the outbreak, but they raised questions about whether Nestlé’s safeguards were sufficient at the time of the recall.

Nestlé spokeswoman Laurie MacDonald said the company was cooperating with federal regulators and had taken corrective steps at the Danville facility. She said Nestlé remained committed to the safety of its products and noted that the company had resumed operations only after reviewing procedures and making improvements.

The recall affected multiple varieties of Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough sold across the United States. The company and federal health officials advised consumers to discard the recalled dough and not attempt to bake or eat it.

The outbreak also renewed public-health warnings about raw cookie dough, which can contain ingredients such as flour and eggs that may carry harmful bacteria. While many consumers associate *E. coli* primarily with meat or produce, investigators have increasingly scrutinized flour and other dry ingredients as possible sources of contamination.

Federal officials said the case highlighted a broader food-safety challenge: products intended to be cooked may still pose risks if consumers eat them raw. Nestlé later emphasized label warnings instructing customers not to consume raw dough and said it continued working to strengthen its food-safety systems.

**FDA finds E. coli in Nestlé Toll House cookie dough as outbreak investigation widens**

Federal health officials say the investigation into an outbreak of **E. coli O157:H7** linked to **Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough** has intensified after FDA testing found the bacteria in a sample of the product, while the CDC reported dozens of illnesses across the country.

The **Centers for Disease Control and Prevention** said the outbreak has sickened people in multiple states, with patients ranging from young children to adults. Many of those infected reported eating raw refrigerated cookie dough before becoming ill. A significant number of patients have been hospitalized, and several have developed **hemolytic uremic syndrome**, a serious complication that can cause kidney failure. No deaths have been reported.

The **Food and Drug Administration** said testing detected **E. coli O157:H7** in a sample of Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough collected during the investigation. Officials said additional laboratory work was being conducted to determine whether the strain found in the product matches the outbreak strain identified in patients. Investigators have been examining the company’s production facility, ingredients, and distribution records to determine how contamination may have occurred.

Nestlé has issued a voluntary recall of its **Toll House refrigerated cookie dough products**, including multiple varieties, sizes, and package types. The recall does not include Nestlé Toll House morsels, already-baked cookies, ice cream, or other products not sold as refrigerated dough. The company also suspended production of the recalled dough while the investigation continues.

Health officials are urging consumers to **throw away any recalled Nestlé Toll House refrigerated cookie dough** and not attempt to bake or eat it. They also emphasized a broader warning: **do not eat raw cookie dough or any raw dough or batter**, whether homemade or commercially produced, because it may contain harmful bacteria from raw ingredients such as flour or eggs.

E. coli O157:H7 can cause severe stomach cramps, bloody diarrhea, and vomiting. Most people recover within a week, but young children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems face a higher risk of serious complications. Consumers who have eaten the recalled dough and developed symptoms are advised to contact a health care provider.
